uncited: Parallel Coordinate Plots (PCP) Generation visualizes the joint distribution of two scalar attributes by mapping nonzero entries in a 2D joint histogram to geometric primitives (quads) on parallel axes.

It differs from point-based scatter plots by using quads to represent histogram bin occupancy, providing a denser and more intuitive representation of material boundaries in volume rendering transfer function design.
This method builds on [Line-based Histogram for 2D Scalar Pairs](6702-line-based-histogram-for-2d-scalar-pairs.md) by utilizing the underlying 2D histogram data structure.
*   **Input:** A 2D joint histogram texture `texcond` of size $W \times H$, where each pixel $P(i, j)$ stores the count $v(i, j)$ of samples falling into bin $(i, j)$ for attributes $x$ and $y$.
An input color $C_0(i, j)$ associated with the bin.
*   Transform Feedback Buffer: GPU memory buffer storing the generated vertex/quad data.
Initialize the transform feedback buffer to record geometry.
Loop through all pairs of conditional histograms (or the single joint histogram slice).
For each histogram slice, draw a regular grid of vertices with dimensions matching the histogram texture size ($W \times H$).
*   Sample the histogram value $v(i, j)$ from `texcond`.
The quad starts at position $i$ on the PC axis for attribute $x$ and ends at position $j$ on the PC axis for attribute $y$.
*   Compute the final color $C(i, j)$ using the formula below.
*   Output the quad with the computed color.
Store all generated quads in the transform feedback buffer.
Render the quads directly from the transform feedback buffer to the screen without reading back to the CPU.
*   $v(i, j)$ is the count in the histogram bin $(i, j)$.
*   $\Sigma v$ is the sum of all values in the histogram (total voxel count).
*   $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm.
*   Histogram resolution: Determined by the size of `texcond`.
*   Color modulation: Based on the log-ratio of bin count to total count.
*   **Zero Values:** Pixels with $v(i, j) = 0$ are skipped and do not generate geometry.
The `draw_grid` call triggers the geometry shader for each vertex.
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of histogram pixels $W \times H$, as each pixel is processed once in the geometry shader.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Proportional to the number of nonzero histogram entries, as only quads for $v(i, j) > 0$ are generated and stored.
No CPU-GPU data transfer is required for the geometry generation step.
*   **Strengths:** Efficient generation of dense visualizations; handles high dynamic range via logarithmic color modulation; direct rendering from GPU memory.
The visual density may become overwhelming for very large histograms.
*   **When to use:** When designing transfer functions for volume rendering and needing to visualize the joint distribution of two scalar attributes efficiently.
*   **When not to use:** When interactive exploration requires rapid updates and the histogram size is extremely large, potentially causing GPU bottlenecks.
It is part of a broader framework for multivariate transfer function design in volume rendering, specifically within the context of probabilistic and statistical modeling of scalar data.
The approach leverages GPU hardware acceleration to generate complex visualizations from statistical data (histograms) without CPU intervention.
